title: JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE:JPM) Shares Climb 4.2% - Still a Buy? - MarketBeat

title: Is your portfolio keeping up? The case for alternatives. - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:

This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button. SITARA SUNDAR: The world is rewiring how it builds, invests, and grows. Is your portfolio keeping up? For decades, investing came down to two tools-- stocks for growth and bonds for stability. Those tools still matter, but their job is getting harder as three forces come together-- economic nationalism, technology adoption, and capital rewiring. The result, more uneven growth, more frequent supply shocks, and inflation, rates, and market swings that stay more volatile than we got used to. That's why we think alternatives can play a strategic role in a portfolio, not as a short-term trade, but as part of the long-term plan. And today, they play two critical roles. Role number 1, broaden your growth engine. Since ChatGPT launched, roughly half of the S&P 500 returns have come from the Magnificent Seven-- Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, NVIDIA, and Tesla. It's been a great run. It also means that much of a typical portfolio is riding on a single theme. Private equity provides access to global return streams that differ from the index. Consider this. About 40% is outside of the US when you think about global private equity, and about 3/4 is outside of tech. It also reaches a much bigger universe of companies. 85% to 95% of companies worldwide with more than $100 million in revenue are private. And companies are staying private longer. Today's typical tech company is about 1 and 1/2 times older and 4 and 1/2 times bigger at IPO than in the '90s. The bottom line, by the time a company rings the opening bell, much of its early growth may have already happened. And that matters even more as AI enters its next chapter. As AI moves beyond tech and into the real economy, the opportunity widens. And many of those businesses are private. In a higher for longer world, cheap debt can't do the heavy lifting anymore. Returns have to come from actually growing the business. Companies that put AI to work in their day-to-day operations could get an extra boost. And for investors looking to invest in the next wave of innovation, the next frontier, that's where access to venture and growth plays a critical role. Role number 2, expand your diversification. For years when stocks fell, bonds caught you. That's no longer a given. With rolling inflation shocks and bigger rate swings, our long-term capital market assumptions expect a higher correlation between stocks and bonds over the next 10 to 15 years. , the largest bank in the United States, opened the third-quarter earnings season with higher profit and a raised outlook for net interest income. For readers following US Financial Stocks, the results offered an early read on the health of consumers, corporate borrowers and capital markets. Earnings per share came in slightly below consensus, partly because of losses on investment securities that management described as discretionary. Excluding that item, profit and returns were stronger, and the underlying business performed well across most lines. Net interest income, the difference between what the bank earns on loans and investments and what it pays on deposits, grew at a healthy pace. Higher deposit balances, growth in credit card lending and larger wholesale loan balances all contributed. The bank raised its full-year net interest income forecast and provided a preliminary outlook for next year that implies further growth. That early guidance was one of the clearest positives in the report, giving investors visibility into a core earnings stream. Management noted that lower interest rates have partially offset balance growth. Even so, rising loan and deposit volumes have more than compensated so far, a sign that the bank's scale allows it to grow income even as rates move against it. Consumer and community banking delivered solid profit growth. Card spending volumes increased, active mobile users grew and the card and auto business expanded on higher balances and lease income. These trends suggest American consumers continue to spend despite higher living costs. Credit quality remained manageable. The provision for credit losses fell from a year earlier, indicating the bank sees no sharp deterioration in borrower health for now. Equity trading had its best third quarter on record, helped by strong activity across products, especially prime services and derivatives. Fixed income trading, by contrast, declined from a year earlier. Investment banking fees rose compared with last year but fell from the previous quarter. The first half of the year included some very large deals, and activity slowed in the second half of September. Management said the pipeline remains strong but expects some transactions to be delayed. Asset and wealth management benefited from strong net inflows and higher market levels, lifting fees. Client asset inflows were large, reflecting the bank's ability to attract money from both wealthy individuals and institutions. This business offers relatively stable fee income that does not depend heavily on interest rates, adding balance to the overall earnings mix. One of the most debated parts of the report was capital. Share repurchases fell sharply from the previous quarter, even though profit remained strong, and the bank's capital ratio slipped compared with a year earlier. The decision suggests management is preserving capital for growth, regulatory changes or market uncertainty. Expenses rose meaningfully, driven by compensation, marketing and technology investment. Controlling cost growth while investing for the future will remain a balancing act. The commercial and investment bank posted strong profit growth, with revenue in banking and payments rising at a double-digit pace. Treasury services, which help companies move money and manage cash, benefit from higher deposit balances and growing transaction volumes. JPMorgan remained the global leader in investment banking fees by wallet share, a position that supports its relationships with large corporations and gives it an edge when deal activity recovers. Payments is increasingly a strategic focus. The bank processes enormous volumes for merchants and corporations, and its scale in this area provides steady fee income that complements lending. Higher borrowing costs may eventually slow loan demand or raise defaults. Further declines in deal activity or fixed income trading would weigh on fee income. Regulatory capital rules also influence how much the bank can return to investors. Geopolitical tension and high energy prices have also held back some corporate transactions, a factor that may affect investment banking through the end of the year. As one of the most influential members of the NYSE Composite, JPMorgan sets the tone for the banking sector. Its results suggest the US economy remains resilient, with consumers spending and companies borrowing. Investors will watch whether dealmaking rebounds, whether net interest income meets the raised outlook and how management approaches capital returns in the coming quarters. The bank also continues to invest heavily in technology, including AI tools that support customer service, fraud detection and internal efficiency. These investments raise expenses today but are designed to keep the bank competitive as digital banking and payments evolve. Market reaction was relatively calm, as the earnings shortfall was largely explained by the discretionary securities losses, while the raised interest income outlook offered reassurance about future profit. title: J.P. Morgan Snags Merrill Lifer Managing $940 Million in Los Angeles - AdvisorHub
content: J.P. Morgan Wealth Management on Friday hired a Merrill Lynch lifer who managed $940 million in assets in Los Angeles, according to an announcement from the hiring firm. J. Embat, a treasury and cash management fintech that uses AI, has integrated the new Banking Authorization Service (BAS) API introduced by J.P. Morgan Payments for treasury services and payments. Through the integration, clients of both companies can connect their J.P. Morgan bank accounts to Embat’s treasury management platform without IT development. The integration targets one of the more time-consuming stages of treasury system implementation: establishing a secure, authenticated connection between the platform and the bank. Connecting a treasury platform to a bank has typically required certificates obtained through an external certification authority. The process involves implementation work, data validation, and signatures, and can take months before a client is able to begin operations. Under the new set-up, joint clients can authenticate and link their J.P. Morgan accounts to Embat’s platform in seconds. According to Antonio Berga, Co-CEO and Co-Founder of Embat, the full process now becomes operational within days rather than months, as clients only need to sign the legal documentation authorising Embat to access their accounts. For treasury teams, this moves bank connectivity from a technical implementation project to a documentation-based authorisation step, reducing the operational effort tied to account activation. J.P. Morgan Payments gives treasury management platforms real-time access to financial data held in J.P. Morgan accounts. With the integration in place, balances, transactions, and payment data flow directly into Embat’s platform, where they are integrated with a company’s enterprise resource planning (ERP) system and wider finance stack. The set-up is particularly relevant for organisations operating multiple subsidiaries or legal entities. Instead of repeating the bank connection process for each entity, finance teams can rely on J.P. Morgan Payments’ single multi-tenant certificate management connection, which uses one security configuration to cover multiple subsidiaries. This allows all corporate entities to be onboarded and managed through a single connection. Embat is also set to become the first treasury management system (TMS) to use J.P. Morgan Payments’ own user interface through the API integration. Morgan Payments, said the focus is on enabling technology providers and their clients to connect to its services as quickly as possible while maintaining the rigour required for every connection. Antonio Berga noted that bank connectivity has long been a time-consuming process for finance teams. Once live, clients can base decisions on real-time data supported by Embat’s AI technology, combined with the security framework of the bank. The integration reflects a broader shift in how banks and TMS providers handle connectivity, with API-based authorisation replacing certificate-driven processes that have traditionally slowed onboarding. For corporate treasury teams, particularly those managing complex group structures, the removal of per-entity connection work and IT development requirements addresses a recurring barrier to adopting treasury platforms. Whalen Global Advisors finds America’s largest banks slipping in the rankings as investors reassess credit risk, rates, and exposure to other financial markets. ESTERO, FL, UNITED STATES, November 4, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Wall Street’s largest banks are reporting strong earnings, but Whalen Global Advisors’ (WGA) proprietary ranking model tells a different story. JPMorgan Chase (JPM), the nation’s largest bank, ranks 49th in WGA’s Q4 2026 rankings, while smaller institutions lead. The average stock in WGA’s 102-bank test group declined 0.56% over the past 200 days amid concerns about interest rates, consumer credit costs, AI-related investments and private credit. None of the largest U.S. banks made the top 10. WGA’s proprietary five-factor model combines fundamental financial and market measures to identify strengths and weaknesses that earnings or share-price performance alone may obscure. “Despite the strong results seen from large cap banks in Q3 2026, the group continues to significantly underperform the broad market,” notes WGA Chairman Christopher Whalen. “Toronto Dominion (TD) is in the number one spot, followed by Bank of Montreal (BMO), Flagstar (FLG) and State Street (STT). None of the top seven depositories are in the top 25 stocks this quarter.” JPMorgan ranked among WGA’s top 10 in 2025, and its shares have gained approximately 14% over the past year. Its fall to 49th illustrates why size and share-price gains do not necessarily translate into strength across the model’s measures. Gold Withdrawals Add Another Dimension to JPMorgan’s Story In September, approximately 3.7 million ounces of eligible gold inventory were reportedly withdrawn from JPMorgan’s New York COMEX vaults, according to analyst David Jensen. The withdrawals reduced stored inventory; they were not a trading loss for the bank. Speaking at the Economic Club of Chicago in October, JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon defended the security of gold stored in the United States, citing its geography, military and rule of law. The withdrawals do not explain JPMorgan’s ranking, but the episode adds to questions about confidence in major financial institutions.Citigroup (C) gained approximately 21% over the past year but ranks 81st. Wells Fargo (WFC) ranks 27th and Bank of America (BAC) 73rd. Toronto-Dominion, ranked first, gained more than 50% over the past year and trades at approximately 2.5 times book value. Whalen believes higher rates and bank exposure to AI-related credit and private lending are weighing on the sector. The AI selloff has raised questions about where institutional capital will move next. “Energy, consumer staples, real estate and utilities are some of the few sectors that are up at present,” notes Whalen. “We exited our positions in several large cap names in Q3 and have since put down some short positions on consumer lenders based upon our belief that consumer credit costs are headed higher.” The rankings raise a central question: are strong quarterly earnings masking risks that will emerge as credit conditions change? By completing this form, you agree to receive marketing communications from PYMNTS and to the sharing of your information with our sponsor, if applicable, in accordance with our Privacy Policy and Terms and Conditions. “Cash application has historically been a necessary but often labor-intensive part of the receivables process,” the release said. “Once a payment arrives, accounts receivable teams must determine which invoices it belongs to, verify remittance information and resolve discrepancies before cash can be applied correctly.” Reconciliation has become complex as businesses receive more payments across a growing range of payment types and channels, according to the release. That means companies often get bogged down by manually moving between systems and matching data, time that could be spent on higher-value strategic efforts. With the Receivables Matching solution, companies can use “configurable matching technology to automatically match incoming payments, remittance information and open accounts receivable data,” the release said. By integrating these data sources, “businesses can reduce manual effort, accelerate cash application and improve visibility into receivables activity.” “Receivables Matching simplifies one of the most complex and bifurcated parts of the receivables process by combining matching, exception management and reporting into one solution built entirely in-house by J.P. Morgan Payments,” Michelle Conklin, the company’s head of receivables and public sector, said in the release. “For clients, that means greater automation without having to replace the technology they already use, helping them operate more efficiently while gaining greater visibility into incoming cash flow.” Chief financial officers are chasing a more optimized and automated reconciliation process,” PYMNTS reported in August. A payment that carries a persistent customer identifier, invoice reference, virtual account identity or structured remittance information can arrive with much of the context already needed to process it. title: 200 days into the frontier: What we know and what to do now - JPMorganChase
content: See how our clients and partners—from small business owners to workforce training leaders—work with JPMorganChase to drive meaningful impact and economic growth where they live and work. Veteran’s Unconventional Path to Landing her Dream Job in Tech U.S. Army Veteran Ashley Wigfall transitioned to a civilian role and charted her path to technologist through mentorship and skills training at the JPMorgan Chase tech hub in Plano, Texas. Chairman and CEO Letter to Shareholders By the JPMorganChase Global Technology Leadership Team More than 200 days into the Super Intelligence era, the implications for business are becoming clearer. Technology is accelerating offense and complexity faster than many enterprises can reduce accumulated risk. Capabilities once limited by specialized expertise are becoming more accessible. Vulnerability discovery and attack automation are moving at warp speed. Remediation is not. At the same time, the frontier’s rapid advancement is increasing dependence on hardware, data centers, telecommunications, water and power. We are all increasingly interconnected, which means resilience ultimately depends on how well the whole ecosystem works together. Earlier this year, we shared 10 actions that enterprises can take to strengthen cyber resilience. Those actions remain important foundations. What is now clearer is that AI magnifies risks accumulated over time. Complexity itself has become a security risk. We are already seeing that critical vulnerabilities can trigger urgent, large-scale remediation efforts. Technology that is outdated or unsupported can become a liability overnight. And as companies race to deploy AI agents, security has to advance with it. For CEOs, the imperative is clear: Change assumptions, shorten decision cycles and build resilience. Reduce accumulated technology risk while ensuring that products and infrastructure being built today are secure and resilient by design. Practices and risks that were acceptable in a former technology environment may no longer be tolerable. When technology and threats move faster, tolerance for avoidable risk has to change too. Outdated technology, internet-facing systems and remediation timelines designed for a slower environment can become liabilities with little warning. Leaders need to reset risk appetite, make exceptions explicit, fund the necessary change and establish accountability across product, technology, security, operations and suppliers. That does not mean treating every problem as equally urgent. It means acting decisively where exposure and potential impact are greatest and directing resources accordingly. Challenge the notion that stable technology is safe technology. Software or hardware can continue to operate while becoming progressively harder to protect. When vendors or software maintainers stop supporting older technology, security patches will stop too. This is known as end of support (EOS). EOS is predictable. Accepting the risk is a choice. PHP illustrates the issue. When serious vulnerabilities emerged, security fixes were provided only for the current version. Organizations running older versions had to move to current or remove the dependency. The same principle applies to unsupported programming platforms, open-source libraries, operating systems and aging hardware. Unsupported technology should be treated as a time-sensitive business liability. Any exception should have an accountable owner, funding, compensating controls and a dated exit plan. Start with a complete, current inventory of software and hardware. Then prioritize by asking three questions: Keeping perimeter technology patched is necessary, but not sufficient. Firewalls, virtual private network gateways and other remote-access technologies connect internal systems to the internet. Because they are directly reachable, a serious vulnerability can give attackers a path into the enterprise. Recent Citrix vulnerabilities underscored that risk, but the architectural issue extends beyond any single product. Patching the vulnerability in front of you addresses today’s exposure. If critical technology remains directly exposed to the internet, the next vulnerability can recreate the same risk. Companies should reduce direct exposure and add layers of protection. An independent authentication layer can prevent unauthenticated traffic from reaching the underlying service, making vulnerabilities harder to discover or exploit. This graphic is divided into two stacked panels that compare system security before and after adding an Auth Filter. The top panel, labeled "Without an Auth Filter," shows the system itself acting as the front door. Two figures, employees and customers on one side and attackers and AI-driven scanning on the other, both have a direct open path to a single box labeled "Internet-facing system," which contains an exposed sign-in page and applications and data. A caption notes that anyone on the internet can reach the sign-in page, and one unpatched flaw there can open a path into the enterprise before anyone has signed in. The bottom panel, labeled "With an Auth Filter," inserts a new middle layer between users and the system. This middle box, titled "Independent security layer at the edge," contains three sequential steps: Screen (block known attacks, floods, and bad bots), Verify (sign in with multi-factor authentication), and Authorize (allow only approved people). Employees and customers pass through this layer via a verified, private link to reach a separate box on the right labeled "Protected system," which is hidden from the internet and contains the same sign-in page and applications and data, now marked as unchanged behind the layer. Attackers and AI-driven scanning are shown being stopped at the edge, with a dotted line indicating that direct connections to the system are refused. Below both panels, three summary callouts state the benefits of this design: less exposure (the system cannot be reached directly from the internet), an independent layer (a flaw in the system alone is not enough to get in), and no single point of failure (the layer is built with redundancy and a tested fallback). In a technology environment, architecture is one of the company’s most consequential security decisions. Product speed and security should not be presented as opposites. Security and resilience requirements should inform market launch, scale and partner selection before architecture becomes difficult or expensive to change. Management teams should understand how a product could be attacked or misused, limit unnecessary access, protect sensitive data and test security throughout development. Unresolved material risk should have clear ownership. Frontier technologies are moving from answering questions to taking action. Agents can increasingly interact with enterprise systems, access information and execute tasks with limited human involvement. Capability, however, should not automatically determine authority. Before expanding what agents can do, establish what they cannot do. Access should be based on the task, not on the theoretical reach of the model. Human oversight should be proportional to consequence: a reversible, low-impact action warrants a different control than moving money, changing production systems or communicating with a customer. Frontier technology is compressing the time between vulnerability discovery, potential exploitation and the need to respond. Governance must be able to move at the speed of the threat. Speed does not mean bypassing governance or accepting uncontrolled change. It is the product of governance designed before the crisis begins. Traditional escalation paths, approval processes and change windows can become risks if they prevent an organization from acting quickly enough. During a significant event, the relevant decision-makers should be clear, escalation thresholds understood, emergency authorities defined and required evidence available quickly. Companies also need the ability to test and deploy critical fixes safely and at speed. Teams should not have to invent a decision process during the incident. Leaders must also be prepared to reprioritize. When new exposure materially changes potential impact, planned work needs to give way and resources need to move with the risk. Risk acceptance should be owned and time-bound. An organization may decide in hours and still require days or weeks to act. It may need to establish which systems are affected, locate accountable owners, test a patch, secure a change window, coordinate suppliers, deploy across a complex estate and confirm that remediation succeeded. Decision speed and execution speed require separate measures. Faster approval has little value if asset data is incomplete, testing capacity is constrained or deployment cannot scale safely. Both the operating model and the technology estate must support rapid action. CEOs should ask whether cyber incident-response teams have the access and authority to act at the speed of an attack, or whether they depend on layers of coordination and approval. When a critical service is exposed and cannot be fixed, teams may also need clear authority to isolate it or take it offline to prevent greater harm. Even the strongest internal process depends on technology suppliers to identify vulnerabilities, communicate them quickly and make fixes available. A supplier can determine how quickly the company responds. Companies should know which providers could become rate-limiting dependencies, whether notification and escalation expectations are contractual, and what options exist if a timely fix is unavailable. An affected service may need to be isolated, replaced or operated temporarily in a reduced state. Exercises should test more than whether a technical team can apply a patch. They should test whether the enterprise can establish exposure, provide executives with decision-useful information, activate emergency authorities, evaluate competing business impacts and deploy safely at scale. Companies cannot predict or prevent every technology disruption. Resilience is the ability to absorb a shock, maintain critical operations and recover with confidence. Every digital service ultimately depends on something physical: hardware, data centers, telecommunications, water and power. AI is increasing dependence on, and demand for, this infrastructure. At the same time, attacks, geopolitical events, energy constraints, supplier concentration and long hardware replacement lead times can create additional points of failure. Companies should understand where single points of failure exist: critical dependencies whose loss could disrupt an essential service without a readily available alternative. That could be a data center, source of power, telecommunications provider, critical hardware component or supplier. The question is whether the business could continue operating if one suddenly became unavailable. Cyber and physical resilience can no longer be managed separately. The disciplined response has three steps: identify the dependency, evaluate the business impact of its loss and act where the potential impact warrants it. Not every dependency requires full duplication. Investment should reflect potential impact, recovery objectives, replacement lead times and the practicality of alternatives. The CEO’s role is to ensure that the largest concentrations are visible and that accepted exposure is deliberate Continuity plans cannot compensate for architecture that allows one weakness, supplier failure or infrastructure disruption to put critical operations at risk. Resilience must be built into products and services, then proven through testing. Design critical services to contain failure, preserve essential functions and recover without relying on the component that failed. Use segmentation and containment to limit impact, build redundancy where warranted, design for graceful degradation and establish viable alternatives that can be activated within the required business timeframe. Then test it. Plans and executive assurance do not demonstrate resilience. Testing does. Exercise failover and recovery under realistic conditions and prove that critical operations can continue, data can be restored and used, and alternate systems, providers or facilities can carry the required workload. Testing should expose where reality falls short of design: how long recovery actually takes, which services miss their targets, what constraints emerge and what remains unresolved. The goal is not to prove that disruption can always be prevented. It is to prove that the company can take a hit, keep its most critical operations running and recover with confidence. The pace will not slow. More capable models will accelerate vulnerability discovery and exploitation. As these capabilities become more widely available, the volume and complexity of cyber and technology events will increase. Organizations must change with the environment. There is no room for complacency. Assumptions, timelines and controls that worked before need to evolve. Reset the tempo. Identify material risks early, understand the potential impact and be prepared to shift priorities and resources when the risk changes. Move faster on what matters most. The organizations that succeed will not be those that predict every threat. They will be those that reduce accumulated risk, make decisions faster, contain failures when they occur and recover before disruption becomes a crisis. Tier 1 — What AI changes: AI is not necessarily the crisis itself, but it changes how fast, how far, and through what a crisis can spread. Four boxes lay out the underlying shifts: Speed (vulnerability discovery is accelerating, but remediation is not), Autonomy (AI agents gain access and authority without equal certainty they will act as intended), Scale (risks that once seemed tolerable can become material quickly), and Dependency (more reliance on hardware, data centers, telecom, water and power). Tier 2 — The CEO response: Three connected black-headed panels linked by arrows show sequential flow. Each panel ends in a boxed "CEO question" prompting a specific leadership check: which assumptions were formed for a world that no longer exists, what would stop the company acting within hours if a material vulnerability emerged tomorrow, and what evidence shows critical services can continue or recover when something fails. Below the three panels, a dashed feedback loop connects all three back to a single rounded callout reading "Learn and adapt: change the control, architecture or decision process that failed," indicating the framework is cyclical rather than linear. Tier 3 — Summary band: A black summary band with three short headers restates the overall intent: Reset the tempo (identify, prioritize and address material risk faster), Adapt decisively (shift resources, tolerances, controls and architecture), and Prove it (show the company can take a hit and keep operating). A closing italic line beneath the graphic reinforces the theme: every action ends in a CEO evidence request, asking management to show it, not assure it. title: The S&P 500 may be headed for 'outsized gains' despite tech-stock rout, JPMorgan says - Business Insider
content: Amid a brutal week in the tech sector, the S&P 500 is flashing one sign better days are coming: improving market breadth. The tech sector is still getting pummeled by fears around AI, but JPMorgan Private Bank sees one bullish signal in the benchmark index that suggests the market is soon headed for a rebound. In a recent note, strategists at the bank pointed to increased market breadth, a measure of the number of winning stocks relative to losing stocks in the S&P 500. For a long time this year, breadth has been narrow, with just a few big names driving the gains at the index level while the majority of stocks struggled. The percentage of stocks in the index that have hit a new 20-day high has risen to over 50%. It's the first time market breadth has risen that high since the second quarter of 2025, around the time the market was making a historic comeback after the tariffs-fueled market crash. The extent to which market breadth has increased recently has historically been followed by more gains in the market over the next three-month and six-month periods, the bank added. JPMorgan recently lifted its year-end target for the S&P 500 to 8,000, implying 5% upside to the index's current levels. "Despite a crowded risk calendar, breadth and historical outperformance sets the US stock market up for outsized returns after the midterm elections," Kriti Gupta, an executive director and global investment strategist in JPMorgan's private bank arm, and Nick Roberts, a portfolio manager at the bank, wrote in a note on Friday. It's been a rough few weeks for US stock investors, with the S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 on track to end October in the red amid several rounds of heavy selling in the AI trade. Fears around AI capex have been widespread and run in multiple directions: investors worry that Big Tech firms may be spending too much on artificial intelligence, and, on the other hand, fear that a pullback in spending could trigger a cascade of consequences that will crush suppliers in the data center space. Deteriorating market breadth was one of the first warnings investors got that not all was well with the AI trade. Several weeks ago, the benchmark indexes were hovering near record highs, but more than 80% of the S&P 500 had slipped into correction territory. The breadth decline was interpreted by strategists as damage building up underneath the market's surface. Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters. More analysts are eyeing a market as the market moves closer to the midterm elections, which has historically been a clearing event that allows stocks to renew their rally once its over. In the six months after the midterms, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 14% since 1970, according to an analysis from BlackRock. In the meantime, the tech sell-off continued on Friday as investors balked at Amazon's and Intel's latest earnings reports, with both tech giants signaling that capex spending would increase next year despite negative cash flow. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down around 8% from its October peak. The iShares Semiconductor ETF, meanwhile, has plunged 28% from its 2026 high, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF is down 43% from its latest peak.

title: The 'haunted' housing market's real problem may be too few people, not too few homes, says J.P. Morgan’s David Kelly - Fortune
content:
“The housing market is haunted,” according to David Kelly, the chief global strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. He lists the ghosts in his widely read Oct. 26 research note: more than a decade of too-easy money, tariffs, and immigration policies that raise the cost of building homes while limiting the number of people who need them, and a Fed whose rate swings hit housing harder than almost anything else. The one that should get the most attention is the people who aren’t showing up. Kelly said he expects U.S. population growth of just 800,000 a year over the next few years. With an average household of about 2.5 people, he writes, that “implies a demographic need for just 320,000 new housing units per year,” compared with roughly 1 million per year in the first two decades of this century. That cuts against the story most Americans have heard about housing: that the country simply hasn’t built enough. Zillow estimated in July the U.S. was about 4.7 million homes short as of 2024, based on how many families are doubled up with unrelated people compared with how many homes sit vacant for rent or sale. Kelly’s read is that the country is “still in a situation of net excess supply.” Thursday’s GDP report bore that out, Kelly told Fortune by email. Homebuilding fell again in the third quarter, “marking the 8th decline in residential construction in the last 10 quarters.” But “the homebuilding decline is still relatively modest compared to the very fast increase in AI-related capital spending,” he said. In the first 20 years of this century, Kelly wrote, the U.S. population grew by an average of 2.4 million people a year—about 1.5 million from births minus deaths and about 900,000 from net immigration. The natural increase peaked at 520,000 in 2025, he writes, and has likely resumed a steady decline as the population ages and birth rates fall. Immigration swung harder. Net international migration fell to 1.3 million in the year through July 2025 from 2.7 million a year earlier, and the Census Bureau projected it would be about 321,000 by July 2026 if trends continued. Kelly estimated that deportations are now almost canceling out legal net immigration, which is still positive but smaller. He said he expects that to hold “regardless of the outcome of the midterm elections,” because enforcement is largely up to the administration, and Congress and the White House are unlikely to agree on an immigration reform bill. Kelly pointed to vacancies. Over the past four years, he writes, the rental vacancy rate rose from 5.6% to 7.3%, and the homeowner vacancy rate from 0.8% to 1.2%. Census figures released Wednesday put rental vacancy at 7.6% in the third quarter, up from 7.1% a year earlier. Between the second quarter of 2024 and the second quarter of 2026, he writes, the housing stock grew by about 2.8 million units. Buyers have thinned out. The National Association of Home Builders’ measure of buyer traffic fell to 18 in October, its lowest level since April 2012 excluding the start of the pandemic, and 43% of builders cut prices. Kelly expects housing starts of 1.32 million this year, the weakest since 2019, falling to 1.24 million in 2027. Others see demand cooling, too. Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies said in June that household growth “has slowed sharply” and that reduced immigration is expected to dampen housing demand further. A Mortgage Bankers Association white paper projects 8.6 million new households from 2025 to 2035, down from 10.1 million in 2010 to 2020. Fewer buyers haven’t meant cheaper mortgages. The 30-year fixed rate averaged 7.32% last week, according to Freddie Mac. Kelly notes that’s below its 50-year average of 7.68%. From January 2008 to December 2021, the rate averaged just 4.15%. “It is important to recognize that this period was the anomaly, rather than today,” he writes, and there’s “little reason to believe that mortgage rates will fall much below 7.0%” without a recession. Kelly said he expects the Fed to raise rates in December and thinks weak housing could make that the last hike of this cycle. What would change his mind, he told Fortune, is if “wage growth suddenly picked up,” or if inflation expectations priced into Treasury inflation-protected securities “were to rise significantly.” Builders are squeezed from both sides. Construction workers are hard to find, Kelly writes, and wages in the industry are rising faster than elsewhere, partly because of the swing in immigration and partly because data-center construction is competing for the same workers. Tariffs and the same infrastructure boom have pushed up the cost of materials. Kelly told Fortune it’s hard to put a number on how much the AI boom is adding to the cost of building a home. But spending on data centers rose 73% in the year through August, to an annual rate of $85 billion, he said, and “it is likely that the resource squeeze from data centers will intensify in 2027.” The ghosts are hardest on the young. Homeownership has fallen since 2022, Kelly writes, “with a much sharper recent decline for those under age 35.” He calls it a decline that is “postponing the reasonable aspirations of young people to be able to marry, settle down and build a family in their own home.” Asked whether that drop is mostly about mortgage rates, Kelly pointed elsewhere. “I think it is a combination of tougher lending standards and the reality that older households have had more of a chance to accumulate a bigger down payment,” he said.
